It wasn't clear to me whether you wanted a vector with the number of matches in each element, a single number with the total number of matches, or a new column within the data frame with the number of matches in each row. Here's how I might have approached each one, using packages not featured in QCLWR. The packages load the magrittr package, which enables the use of the forward pipe operator %>%, which can take some time to get accustomed to, but increases the (sequential) readability of the code (as opposed to an inside-out way of writing several functions).

x <- c("i love the carbon tax.",
       "carbon tax, carbon tax.",

       "idea for the carbon tax: great carbon tax, a carbon tax people can live with.",

       "nothing to see here.")

corpus <- data.frame(sentences=x)

# loads sweet packages
library("stringr")
library("dplyr")

# returns vector with number of matches in each element
str_extract_all(corpus$sentences, "carbon tax") %>% sapply(length)

# returns single number with total matches
str_extract_all(corpus$sentences, "carbon tax") %>% sapply(length) %>% sum()

# creates new column in data frame with number of matches in each record
corpus <- corpus %>% mutate(num_matches = str_extract_all(.$sentences, "carbon tax") %>% sapply(length))

Bob, try this reproducible example (that is, an example that you can copy and paste directly into R), after you've installed "stringr" and "dplyr":

### START REPRODUCIBLE EXAMPLE ###

# creates toy data frame
df <- data.frame(
  id = 1:4,
  sentence = c("i love the carbon tax.", "carbon tax, carbon tax.", "idea for the carbon tax: great carbon tax, a carbon tax people can live with.", "nothing to see here.")
)

# loads sweet packages
library("stringr")
library("dplyr")

# summarizes number of matches by id
df %>% group_by(id) %>% summarise(num_matches = str_count(sentence, "carbon tax"))

### END EXAMPLE ###

Obviously, you'll need to change "id" in "group_by(id)" to the exact name of the variable with the id in your data frame, and "sentence" in "str_count(sentence, "carbon tax")" to the exact name of the variable with the sentences. Note that those variable names should not have spaces in them.

As Stefan was alluding to, there is a difference between the function definition and a function call.

# This is a function definition.
myfun <- function(a, b, c){
  return(a+b+c)
}

# This is a function call.
myfun(1, 2, 3)

In R, options with an '=' have a default, so usually if there is an option you don't understand but it has a default, you may not have to worry about it.

Don't let one or two obscure sentences stop you from using what is an amazingly flexible and powerful open-source tool such as R.

Someone with more corpus linguistics knowledge can answer far better than myself (I'm more of a general R hacker), but zero-length position suggests to me that it is sort of "in-between" space between two characters, and so is a somewhat abstract "word boundary." For example in "this phrase" there is a word boundary after the "s" and before the space; the "s" is the fourth character and the space is the fifth character, and the word boundary is a character of zero length between the fourth and the fifth character. What the function actually returns, I don't know, but whatever it is, it better have zero-length because it is a sort of invisible boundary. Again, someone with more knowledge can probably answer better, this is just a guess.

The short explanation:

·         all strings are sequences of characters.

·         Their length is counted as the n of characters they contain.

·         a “zero length” string is one where there are 0 characters in the string

o    i.e. the string ends instantly as soon as it starts; its start point and end point are the same place

·         In regular expressions, there are assorted wildcards like . \w \s and so on, that can “match” substrings of different length.

·         For instance, in the regex “one.*another”, the length of the substring matched by “.*” can be anything from zero upwards.

o    IF it matches against “one&another”, its length is 1

o    IF it matches against “one-and-another”, its length is 5

o    IF it matches against “oneanother”, its length is 0

·         There are also regex wildcards which always match zero length

·         the “\b” wildcard matches a word boundary – i.e. the boundary between one or more word characters, and one or more not-word characters

·         because it matches a boundary between characters rather than actual characters, its match is always zero characters in length.

·         … which is what I believe the tutorial you mentioned was referring to.

This is all about the nature of strings/regex in general rather than R specifically though. There is a lot of support material out there on the web on regex…

best

Andrew.
